analysis.one_liner: Requires clemency recipients to disclose money and gifts they gave to the President, his family, and his businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would force pardon recipients to disclose payments to the President and his family, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since its August 2026 referral with no action and no Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone who receives a federal pardon, commutation, or reprieve to tell the Justice Department about any money, gifts, or other benefits of $10,000 or more they provided to the President, his family, or businesses and committees tied to them. Those disclosures would be posted on a public, searchable Justice Department website. It would also spell out in federal bribery law that a pardon counts as a "thing of value" and extend to 10 years the time prosecutors have to bring bribery charges connected to clemency.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want to know whether pardons were bought would gain a searchable public record: anyone who receives a federal pardon, commutation, or reprieve would have to disclose payments, gifts, contracts, or investments of $10,000 or more provided to the President, his immediate family, or entities tied to them — including businesses, the presidential library or foundation, campaign committees, and any entity the recipient knows the President's family has a financial stake in — and the Justice Department would publish those reports online [S2]. Federal bribery law would be updated to state explicitly that a pardon is a "thing of value," that the President and Vice President count as covered officials, and that bribery charges tied to clemency can be brought within 10 years instead of the standard window [S2]. People who use the regular Justice Department clemency process would benefit indirectly from a system less tilted toward those who can pay [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public, searchable Justice Department database of payments and benefits (over $10,000 in a 12-month period) that pardon recipients provided to the President, his family, or entities tied to them, covering the year before the President took office through four years after the clemency is granted.

Amends the federal bribery statute to state explicitly that a pardon, commutation, or reprieve is 'anything of value' and that the President and Vice President count as the officials it covers, removing arguments that trading money for clemency falls outside the law.

Extends the statute of limitations to 10 years for bribery offenses connected to the granting, promising, or withholding of executive clemency, and extends the same 10-year window to the new disclosure requirement.

Backs the disclosure rule with teeth: civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation and up to five years in prison for willfully failing to file or filing false reports, with the Justice Department empowered to investigate and enforce.

analysis.who_pays: People who receive federal clemency would bear the compliance cost: anyone who gave a benefit of $10,000 or more within roughly five years of the grant to the President, his family, or entities tied to them would have to file disclosure reports with the Justice Department, on pain of civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation or criminal penalties of up to five years for willful violations [S2]. Businesses built around shepherding pardons through political access would see their payments to presidential-linked entities exposed on a public website [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill's findings are built entirely around one president's clemency record, and critics would argue that criminalizing conduct around a constitutionally granted pardon power intrudes on an executive authority the courts have described as broad — which is partly why the bill targets recipients and intermediaries rather than the President himself.

The definitions reach wide: 'covered recipients' include presidential libraries, charities, inaugural committees, campaign committees, and any entity the recipient should know has a presidential family stake, and the covered-benefit threshold of $10,000 could sweep in ordinary donations and gifts, creating legal risk for clemency recipients trying to comply.

Enforcement depends entirely on the Justice Department of the day; the bill gives the Attorney General discretion to investigate and prosecute, so an administration unwilling to police its own clemency grants could simply decline to act.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that disclosure does not prevent a pardon from being traded — it only documents the payments after the fact, and a president facing no criminal exposure could still grant clemency to allies and let the paperwork pile up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is modest and cheap: publish who paid what to the President's circle around a pardon, and make sure bribery law plainly covers clemency. The benefits are real but indirect — the public learns after the fact, and deterrence depends on the Justice Department of the day choosing to enforce. The costs fall on clemency recipients and their lawyers in paperwork and legal risk, and the bill's breadth (charities, libraries, campaign committees, a $10,000 threshold reaching back a year before inauguration) would need careful implementation to avoid punishing legitimate petitioners. The larger limitation is structural: because the Supreme Court has treated the pardon power as core presidential authority, the bill cannot touch the President's own decision, only the money that moves around it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Morelle introduced the No Payoffs for Pardons Act on August 3, 2026.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, which is the only action taken on it in the record.
Nine House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican has cosponsored.

The bill's own findings section states that presidential clemency has been used to reward donors, loyalists, and well-connected offenders, wiping out nearly $2 billion in victim repayments, and that the bill targets the intermediaries and recipients around such arrangements rather than the President's own constitutionally protected conduct.
Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically alive but has not moved past referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has gained or lost anything: the bill sits in committee with the majority party showing no support for it. The status quo — a pardon process with no disclosure of payments from recipients to the President and his circle — continues in the meantime.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill awaits committee action

for.name: Rep. Joseph Morelle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee Republicans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action on it since August 2026.

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: The bill's findings take aim at his clemency practices, and no congressional Republicans support the bill, leaving the majority party with little incentive to move it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 9 cosponsors are House Democrats, and no Republican has signed on to a bill whose findings center on President Trump's clemency practices.

industries.industry: Presidential family business and political-fundraising enterprises
industries.note: The bill would compel public disclosure of payments and gifts from pardon recipients to the President, his family, and their business and political entities, exposing a channel that has operated in the dark. It also closes a gap in bribery law that currently leaves clemency-for-pay arrangements weakly covered.

industries.industry: Clemency lobbying and access services (pardon brokers and law firms selling political access)
industries.note: Payments for clemency-related advocacy and lobbying would become disclosable, with only bona fide court-representation fees exempt. Law firms working the pardon-lobbying space would face new reporting obligations and public scrutiny.

industries.industry: Wealthy clemency recipients and their associates
industries.note: The individuals most directly regulated — clemency recipients who gave large benefits to the President or his circle — are overwhelmingly wealthy and well-connected offenders, including white-collar fraudsters whose pardons the bill says erased nearly $2 billion in victim repayments.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the profile of most measures that die quietly: introduced late in a session, one sponsor, a handful of same-party cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action since referral. Barring an unexpected markup or a political shift that makes clemency transparency a floor priority, it is likely to remain in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
